# Discrete-time Markov chains

The Markov property says that a well-chosen current state carries everything the next state needs from the past. It does not say that successive states are independent. For a queue, the number of customers present can be enough when arrivals and service are memoryless. Under a service law with memory, the elapsed service time has to sit in the state as well. That modelling choice is on [Stochastic processes](sp-01-stochastic-processes.qmd).

The finite-state definition, the Chapman–Kolmogorov product, simulation from a row of $P$, and the theorem that $P^n$ settles to one row for an irreducible aperiodic chain are on [Markov chains](prob-06-markov-chains.qmd). Using a chain to sample from a target distribution is a different construction, on [Markov chains, Gibbs sampling, and Metropolis--Hastings](bayes-04-mcmc.qmd), where the invariant vector is called a stationary distribution. This page keeps the transition-matrix notation and goes further: hitting probabilities and mean hitting times, the two-state spectrum, doubly stochastic chains, and the separation between a stationary law and the distribution reached from one start.

## Transition rules

::: {#def-sp-dtmc .definition}
## Discrete-time Markov chain

A process $X_0,X_1,\ldots$ on a finite or countable state space $S$ is a discrete-time Markov chain when

$$
\Pr(X_{n+1}=j\given X_n=i,X_{n-1},\ldots,X_0)=\Pr(X_{n+1}=j\given X_n=i)=p_{ij}
$$

for every $n$ and every choice of states. The chain is time-homogeneous when $p_{ij}$ does not depend on $n$. The transition matrix $P=(p_{ij})$ has non-negative entries, and every row sums to $1$.

:::

The finite-state case of this definition is the one on [Markov chains](prob-06-markov-chains.qmd#def-finite-state-markov-chain). Countable $S$ is included here so that a branching process and an unbounded walk fit the same sentence.

If the row vector $\mu_0$ is the law of $X_0$, then $\mu_n=\mu_0 P^n$. The $n$-step probability is $p_{ij}^{(n)}=(P^n)_{ij}$. Conditioning on the state at time $m$ splits a trip of length $m+n$ into a trip of length $m$ and a trip of length $n$:

$$
p_{ij}^{(m+n)}=\sum_{k\in S} p_{ik}^{(m)} p_{kj}^{(n)}.
$$

These are the Chapman–Kolmogorov equations. Matrix multiplication is the sum over every possible intermediate state.

::: {#exm-sp-weather-two-day .example}
## Rain after two days

A two-state weather chain has states sunny and rainy, in that order, and

$$
P=\begin{pmatrix} 0.8 & 0.2 \\ 0.3 & 0.7 \end{pmatrix}.
$$

**Question.** Starting from sun, find the probability of rain two days later. Also find the probability of sun two days after rain.

**Solution.** The sunny-to-rainy entry of $P^2$ sums the two routes through the intermediate day:

$$
(P^2)_{12}=0.8\cdot 0.2+0.2\cdot 0.7=0.30.
$$

The rainy-to-sunny entry is

$$
(P^2)_{21}=0.3\cdot 0.8+0.7\cdot 0.3=0.45.
$$

The two numbers differ. A row-stochastic matrix need not be symmetric, and it need not be column-stochastic. Rows are the current state and columns are the next state. That orientation is the one used with row vectors $\mu_n=\mu_0 P^n$.

:::

A diagram makes impossible moves visible. The chain

$$
P=\begin{pmatrix} 0.7 & 0.3 & 0 \\ 0.2 & 0.5 & 0.3 \\ 0 & 0.4 & 0.6 \end{pmatrix}
$$

moves only between neighbours, or stays. The one-step probability from state $1$ to state $3$ is $0$. The two-step probability is $(P^2)_{13}=0.3\cdot 0.3=0.09$, through state $2$. Reachability is a property of the powers of $P$, not only of the positive entries of $P$ itself.

## Hitting questions use the same principle

The first-step analysis on [Random walks and first passage](sp-03-random-walks.qmd) extends from a path graph to any transition matrix. For a target set $A\subset S$, let $T_A=\inf\{n\ge 0: X_n\in A\}$. For disjoint targets $A$ and $B$, write $h_i=\Pr_i(T_A<T_B)$. Conditioning on the first step gives

$$
h_i=\sum_j p_{ij} h_j \quad(i\notin A\cup B),
\qquad
h_i=1\ (i\in A),
\qquad
h_i=0\ (i\in B).
$$

If the mean hitting time of $A$ is finite, $e_i=\E_i T_A$ solves

$$
e_i=1+\sum_j p_{ij} e_j \quad(i\notin A),
\qquad
e_i=0\ (i\in A).
$$

The $1$ is the step just taken. The sum is the expected remaining time from the next state. On a finite state space these are linear equations, one unknown per state outside the target.

## Stationary distributions

::: {#def-sp-stationary-distribution .definition}
## Stationary distribution

A probability row vector $\pi$ is a stationary distribution of $P$ when $\pi P=\pi$. If $X_0$ has law $\pi$, then $X_n$ has law $\pi$ at every time $n$.

:::

For the weather chain, $\pi_S+\pi_R=1$ and the balance of probability across the two off-diagonal entries is $0.2\pi_S=0.3\pi_R$. Hence $\pi_S=1.5\pi_R$, and $\pi=(0.6,0.4)$. The initial state affects short-run probabilities. It does not appear in the stationary equation.

If $P$ is doubly stochastic, every column sums to $1$ as well as every row. On a finite set with $m$ states the uniform row $(1/m,\ldots,1/m)$ then satisfies

$$
(\pi P)_j=\sum_{i=1}^m \frac{1}{m} p_{ij}=\frac{1}{m},
$$

because column $j$ sums to $1$. Uniformity is stationary. Doubly stochastic is a sufficient condition, not a necessary one: the weather chain has a stationary distribution and its columns do not sum to $1$.

Multiplying by $P$ moves a probability distribution forward one step. A stationary distribution is a fixed point of that map. Whether an arbitrary starting distribution approaches the fixed point is a separate question. The sampling use of the same fixed-point equation is the [stationary distribution](bayes-04-mcmc.qmd#def-stationarity-and-detailed-balance) of a Monte Carlo chain.

## Spectral view for two states

Let

$$
P=\begin{pmatrix} 1-a & a \\ b & 1-b \end{pmatrix}, \qquad a,b>0.
$$

The eigenvalues are $1$ and $1-a-b$. The stationary law is

$$
\pi=\Bigl(\frac{b}{a+b},\frac{a}{a+b}\Bigr).
$$

The second eigenvalue controls the decay of a deviation from $\pi$. Write a starting row as $\pi$ plus a multiple of the left eigenvector for $1-a-b$. After $n$ steps that deviation is multiplied by $(1-a-b)^n$. Whenever $|1-a-b|<1$, which holds as soon as $a$ and $b$ are not both $0$ or both $1$ in the alternating way below, $P^n$ approaches the matrix with every row equal to $\pi$.

At $a=b=1$ the second eigenvalue is $-1$. The chain swaps states at every step, $P^n$ alternates between $P$ and $I$, and the powers have no limit. A stationary distribution still exists: $\pi=(1/2,1/2)$. This is the same two-state alternation as the periodic example on [Markov chains](prob-06-markov-chains.qmd). The eigenvalue makes the oscillation visible: magnitude $1$, and not equal to the eigenvalue $1$.

## The Markov assumption as a chosen state

Suppose tomorrow's weather depends on today's weather and also on whether it has already rained for three days. Two states cannot store a run of length three. A state such as $(\text{today's weather},\text{current run length})$ can. The state space gets larger, and the transition rule becomes local in time again. Compressing the past into a state makes the one-step calculation possible. Compressing too far drops information the next step uses.

Time homogeneity is a separate assumption. A chain can be Markov at every time with a matrix $P_n$ that changes with $n$, for example a morning matrix and an evening matrix. The law is then

$$
\mu_n=\mu_0 P_0 P_1\cdots P_{n-1},
$$

not a power of one matrix. Solving $\pi P=\pi$ for a single matrix does not describe that process.

## Stationarity and the law from one start

If the chain starts from $\pi$, every later marginal equals $\pi$. The path still moves. Stationarity is a statement about marginal distributions, not a claim that the chain freezes.

If the chain starts in a single state $i$, the law $\mu_0 P^n$ may take time to approach $\pi$. In a periodic chain it may fail to approach $\pi$ at individual times, even though $\pi$ exists. The class structure, the period, and the conditions that turn a stationary law into a limit from every start are on [Classes, recurrence, and reversibility](sp-05-classes-and-reversibility.qmd). The limit theorem for an irreducible aperiodic finite chain, with the stepping-stone calculation, is on [Markov chains](prob-06-markov-chains.qmd#thm-limiting-distribution).

::: {.callout-note}
## Key idea
One row of $P$ is the law of the next state given the current state. Hitting probabilities and mean hitting times solve first-step equations with boundary values on the target. A vector $\pi=\pi P$ is unchanged by one step. Convergence of $P^n$ to that vector needs more than the equation $\pi P=\pi$.
:::

## A deterministic three-cycle

A chain on $\{1,2,3\}$ moves from $1$ to $2$, from $2$ to $3$, and from $3$ to $1$, with probability $1$. Find a stationary distribution, and describe $\Pr(X_n=1\given X_0=1)$ as $n$ grows.

[Solution](#sol-sp-deterministic-cycle)
